title: I had an AI agent rig and animate 2D characters from a single painting. The hard part wasn't the rigging, it was that the agent couldn't tell when it had broken one.
author: firejune
selftext: Solo dev here, making a game with web tech, and the part I can't do alone is the CG side. So for the last couple of months I've been testing how much of it an agent can take over: paint a character, cut it into layers, rig it, give it an idle, retarget motion from video. The rigging and animation part became an open-source toolchain, rig-c (MIT, https://github.com/rig-c). This post is about what went wrong and what fixed it, because the fixes are the interesting bit. Demo if you want to see the output first: [https://rig-c.org/examples/](https://rig-c.org/examples/) plays 20 rigs in the browser (five characters cut out of one group illustration, four outfits each; there's a Bones toggle). The problem. In my setup the agent's only feedback was whether the file parsed, and Spine's parser is very forgiving. A constraint written the 4.2 way just vanishes in 4.3. Give a curve four numbers instead of what it wants and you get NaN. A mesh whose vertex count happens to equal its UV count drops its bone weights without a word. The file loads, the agent says "done", and it isn't lying. I'd find out later, when something detached in motion. What fixed it. I stopped treating the rig as something the agent writes and started treating it as something the agent submits to a compiler. The agent writes two JSON files (rig spec, motion spec); rigc checks them against a list of named assertions (36 under the default Spine profile; the parts tool builds under the stricter rig-play profile, which runs all 50) and either writes Spine 4.3 data or writes nothing. No flag to skip the checks. The part that surprised me is how much the wording of the refusals mattered. This is what the agent sees if a part image goes missing: FAIL A17\_ATLAS\_PAGE\_FILES\_EXIST: page "../images/hull.png" is not on disk at …/images/hull.png It says which file it couldn't find and where it looked, so the agent fixes that without reading docs; the checks that measure something name the value found and the value required instead, e.g. a mesh vertex whose weights sum to 0.9000. Either way I ended up spending more time on those lines than on documentation. The other rule that paid off: the compiler never guesses. If a number isn't in the spec it's an error naming the field, not a "reasonable default", which keeps the build record honest about what was actually measured. What it doesn't fix. The checks say the data is structurally valid, nothing about how it looks. A rig with its head next to its torso passes, because those are the numbers the spec asked for. So a person still looks at the end, and the output imports into the Spine editor for exactly that. Motion has a limit too: pushing one drawing through a run or a dance doesn't produce what the drawing never had; mild motion (idle, gesture, walk) retargets fine, intense motion wants replacement drawings. That's measured, not a hunch; the pose tool's README has the table. Does it work for an agent that's never seen it? I run a public exam ( [https://rig-c.org/exam/](https://rig-c.org/exam/) ): a fresh session gets only the installed package's README and --help and has to write down what it expects before each command. On Oct 20, eight models from three families sat all five tasks. Six passed every machine-checked line on the dance task; one person then judged the rendered clips blind and scored those six anywhere from 3 to 9 out of 10. So the checks get a run looked at and say almost nothing about the score. The failed attempts are kept too, in a trials directory, each with the number that sank it. Practical notes if you try it: no GPU needed for any rig-c step and no model weights shipped; the painting and the layer split come from image models you run yourself (See-through for the layer split). The getting-started guide starts from a published example whose painting and layers are already made, Bun only, no Python: [https://rig-c.org/docs/getting-started/](https://rig-c.org/docs/getting-started/) . The player has no Spine runtime; it poses rigid parts as + CSS matrix(), with adapters for Pixi, Phaser and Three. Question for people doing this: when the parser and the validator both pass a rig that still looks wrong, what feedback do you feed back to the agent? I've got "a person looks at the end" and a validator that refuses by name. If you've found something better, I'd like to hear it.

comments.author: songokuthegreat
comments.body:
Thank you for taking time to share and thoroughly explain this exciting pipeline to us!  
It looks very promising, but I’m curious as to whether or not this could be used to model and rig an Arc System Works-styled character (e.g., Guilty Gear Strive / Dragon Ball FighterZ / Kill La Kill IF) with the exact/similar toon shading techniques from scratch? 

I’ve been trying to adopt this style in my own games, but have been unsuccessful in finding an AI pipeline that can be used for this exact purpose instead of outsourcing it to an experienced human 3D modeler/freelancer. Each AI tool that I’ve used for this purpose on previous occasions have produced extremely undesirable results on their own (Tripo, Meshy, BlenderMCP).  

Would appreciate clarification regarding this.

replies.author: firejune
replies.body:
Thanks for the kind words. The honest answer is no, not for the 3D workflow you're describing. rig-c is 2D only: it rigs a painted character using cut-out parts, rather than creating 3D models or toon shaders. It won't replace the modeling and shading work needed for that style.

If a 2D alternative is useful, though, I've recently got a depth-based head-turn demo working. Move your pointer across the character to turn the head and have the eyes follow: [https://rig-c.org/demos/head-turn/](https://rig-c.org/demos/head-turn/)

It uses a depth map to drive actual rotation in 2.5D, rather than just shifting layers for parallax. The range of rotation is limited. It's a preview of an upcoming rig-c feature; the step that builds it from a painting is still in progress.

It doesn't provide full 3D turnarounds or lighting-responsive toon shading, so it isn't a solution to the exact pipeline you're looking for. But if a painted 2D character with a sense of depth could work for your game, it may be worth a look.

replies.author: songokuthegreat
replies.body:
I see! I’m not too disappointed since I know it’s a difficult/unlikely to find and that the technology just isn’t there right now.   
The rig-c you made isn’t quite what I’m looking for, but it’s an incredible idea that really brings static 2D images to life. 

Keep up the excellent work.
